PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

CLASSIFICATION OF KINGDOM

Taxonomy

  • It is the science of describing, naming, and classifying organisms, including all plants, animals, and microorganisms.

Order of Classification

Classification

Two Kingdom Classification

  • Proposed by: Carolus Linnaeus (1758) → "Father of Taxonomy".

Kingdoms:

  • → Plantae: Included all plants, algae, fungi.
  • → Animalia: Included all animals.

Linnaeus published "System Nature" in 1735.

Three Kingdom Classification

  • Proposed by: Ernst Haeckel (1866) → Coined the term "Ecology".

Kingdoms:

  • → Plantae
  • → Animalia
  • → Protista: New kingdom added for unicellular organisms (Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena).

Three Domain Classification

  • Proposed by: Carl Woese (1990).

Domains:

  • → Bacteria: True prokaryotes (E.g. E. coli).
  • → Archaea: Microorganisms with prokaryotic cells that are distinct from bacteria and are often found in extreme environments (E.g. Halobacterium).
  • → Eukarya: All eukaryotic organisms (Protists, Fungi, Plants, Animals).

Five Kingdom Classification

  • Proposed by: R.H. Whittaker (1969).

Kingdoms:

  • → Monera: Prokaryotes (bacteria, blue-green algae).
  • → Protista: Eukaryotic unicellular organisms.
  • → Fungi: Eukaryotic multicellular (some are unicellular) organisms, heterotrophic, spore-producing organisms.
  • → Plantae: Autotrophic, multicellular.
  • → Animalia: Heterotrophic, multicellular.
  • Basis of classification: Cell structure, mode of nutrition, body organization, reproduction.

Types of Classification

  • Cell Nature: Prokaryotes / Eukaryotes
  • Cell Occurrence: Unicellular / Multicellular
  • Mode of Nutrition: Autotrophs / Heterotrophs
  • Level of Body Organization: Cellular / Tissue / Organ / Organ System

KINGDOM MONERA

  • Cell type: Prokaryotic (no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles).
  • Organization: Unicellular, microscopic.
  • Cell Wall: Made up of peptidoglycan (in bacteria).
  • Nutrition: Autotrophic (photosynthetic or chemosynthetic) or heterotrophic (saprophytic or parasitic).

Classification of Kingdom Monera

Monera is mainly divided into two major groups:

  1. 1. Eubacteria (True bacteria)
  • Most common and well-known group of bacteria.
  • Cell wall: Contains peptidoglycan.
  • Nutrition: Mostly heterotrophic (saprophytes, parasites), with some autotrophs (including photoautotrophs like cyanobacteria).
  1. 2. Archaebacteria (Ancient bacteria)
  • They live in extreme environments (hot springs, salt lakes, swamps).
  • Cell wall: Cell wall present but lacks peptidoglycan.

KINGDOM PROTISTA

  • Cell type: Eukaryotic (has a true nucleus and organelles), cell wall is absent.
  • Organization: Mostly unicellular, some are colonial or simple multicellular.
  • Locomotion: Through appendages.

Nutrition:

  • → Autotrophic (photosynthesis): Algae.
  • → Heterotrophic: Protozoans (ingest food).

Habit: Growth form of a plant comprising its shape, size and orientation.

Habitat: Natural home or environment of a plant or animal.

Classification of Kingdom Protista

  1. 1. Phylum Protozoa
  • Cell type: Unicellular.
  • Mode of Nutrition: Heterotrophic (ingest food), parasitic or symbiotic.
  • Habitat: Mostly aquatic, solitary however few are colonial.

E.g. Euglena (uses flagellum for movement), Amoeba (uses pseudopodia, a false-feet for movement), Paramecium (uses cilia for movement, that also helps to move food to its oral cavity), Plasmodium.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

KINGDOM FUNGI

  • Cell Type: Eukaryotic (has a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles).
  • Organization: Mostly multicellular, but some are unicellular (E.g. Yeast).
  • Cell Wall: Present and is made of chitin (not cellulose like in plants).
  • Nutrition: Heterotrophic, typically saprophytic (feed on decaying organic matter), but some are parasitic (dependent on protoplasm of a host organism for food or mutualistic (both benefits from their association and sharing of resources).
  • Some of them are in symbiotic relationship (benefit from each other). E.g. Lichen (Blue-green algae + Fungi) The fungus provides shelter, protection, and access to water and nutrients, while the blue-green algae (or green algae) produce food for the fungus through photosynthesis.

KINGDOM PLANTAE

  • Cell Type: Eukaryotic (has a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles).
  • Organization: Multicellular.
  • Cell Wall: Made up of cellulose (provides structure and support).
  • Nutrition: Autotrophic (producing their own food via photosynthesis, using chlorophyll).

Kingdom Plantae is classified on the basis of:

  • Differentiation of plant body and distinct components.
  • Presence or absence of vascular tissues.
  • Ability to bear seeds.
  • Seeds are enclosed within the fruits.
  • Ability to produce flowers.

Cryptogamae Vs Phanerogamae

CryptogamaePhanerogamae
Seeds, fruits, flowers are absent.Seeds, fruits, flowers are present
Reproductive organs are hidden.Reproductive organs are exposed.
Less evolved plantsHighly evolved plants
E.g. Thallophytes, Bryophytes, and PteridophytesE.g. Gymnosperms and Angiosperms

Phylums of Kingdom Plantae

  1. 1. Thallophyta (Algae)

Phycology: Study of Algae

  • Cell type: Eukaryotic.
  • Simple, do not have well-differentiated body parts such as roots or stem (they have thallus).
  • Non-vascular (no specialized tissue for transporting water and nutrients).
  • Habitat: Mostly aquatic, mostly found in freshwater or marine environments. E.g. Spirogyra, Ulothrix, Ulva, Chara.
  • Movement: Non-motile.
  • Nutrition: Autotrophic, photosynthetic (contain chlorophyll). Different pigments are present (edible or non-edible).

E.g.

  • Chlorophyceae (Green algae): Chlorella (rich in proteins), Spirulina (superfood).
  • Phaeophyceae (Brown algae): Sargassum, Laminaria (Kelp).
  • Rhodophyceae (Red algae): Gelidium, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Polysiphonia.

TRICK TO REMEMBER (Chlorophyceae)

  • U: Ulothrix (SLVCC)

Kelp (mannitol is a sweet alcohol made from Kelp.)

Kingdom Plantae: Cryptogamae (Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta) | Phanerogamae (Gymnosperms, Angiosperms) → Monocots / Dicots

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

  • Agar a jelly like substance, is obtained from Rhodophyceae (red algae).
  1. 2. Bryophyta (Bryophytes)
  • They are known as "Amphibians of plant kingdom" (exists both in land and water).
  • Non-vascular plants → no specialised tissues for water and food conduction (lack xylem and phloem).
  • They have well-differentiated body however lack true roots, stems and leaves. Roots like structure present in bryophytes are called Rhizoids.
  • Nutrition: Autotrophic.
  • Movement: Non-motile.
  • Reproduction: Through spores (no seeds) in water.
  • → Male reproductive part: Antheridium.
  • → Female reproductive part: Archegonium.
  • Habitat: Found in damp and moist areas.

E.g.

  • Mosses: Funaria.
  • Liverworts: Marchantia, Riccia.
  1. 3. Phylum Pteridophyta
  • They are considered as first terrestrial vascular plants (have xylem and phloem).
  • Well-differentiated roots, stems, and leaves (called fronds in ferns). Leaves are made of leaflets that bear spores called Sporophylls.
  • They have hidden reproductive organs (cryptogams).
  • Habitat: Found in cracks of rocks, moist, and shady places.

E.g. Marsilea, Ferns, and Horsetails.

Gymnosperms (Meaning: Gymno (without cover) and Sperma (seeds without fruits))

  • Vascular plants, have true roots, stem and leaves (with xylem and phloem).
  • Phloem Companion and Xylem Vessel are absent.
  • Seed-producing plants, but seeds are naked (not enclosed in fruit). The seeds are primitive and simple.
  • They are usually perennials, evergreen, and mostly woody plants.

E.g. Pines, Deodar, Cycas.

Angiosperms (Meaning: Angio (covered) and Sperma (seeds))

  • They are flowering plants and produce seeds enclosed within fruit (ovary gets modified into fruit).
  • Vascular plants with xylem and phloem. They are highly evolved.
  • Flowers are the reproductive organs.
  • Seeds have embryo inside it and embryos have structure called cotyledons (seed leaves).

Divers group, with two major classes:

  • → Monocots: They have one cotyledon. E.g., grasses, lilies.
  • → Dicots: They have two cotyledons. E.g., roses, sunflowers.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

Remember: Main plant body in Algae and Bryophytes is Gametophyte (n) while in Pteridophytes, Gymnosperms, and Angiosperms, it is Sporophyte (2n).

KINGDOM ANIMALIA

Kingdom Animalia: Invertebrates (without backbone): Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata | Vertebrates (with backbone): Fish, Reptiles, Amphibians, Birds, Mammals

Let's first classify them under certain Parameters!

Kingdom Animalia

  • They are eukaryotic and multicellular organisms.
  • They are heterotrophic.
  • Animal cells lack a rigid cell wall.
  • Mobility: Most animals are capable of movement at some stage of their life cycle.
  • Kingdom Animalia is classified into phylum on the basis of extent and type of body design differentiation found in them.

Body Level Organisation

  • Body level organization refers to the hierarchical arrangement of structures within a living organism, from the smallest units to the entire organism. It involves five main levels: cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and the organism.

On the Basis of Symmetry

  • Asymmetrical: Asymmetry refers to the lack of symmetry in an organism's body plan. E.g. Porifera.
  • Radial Symmetry: In radial symmetry, any plane passing through the central axis divides the organism into two equal halves. E.g. Coelenterata, Echinodermata.
  • Bilateral Symmetry: Bilateral symmetry is characterized by a single plane of symmetry that divides the organism into left and right halves. E.g. Platyhelminthes, Arthropoda.

No Symmetry (e.g., Porifera) | Radial Symmetry (e.g., Cnidaria) | Bilateral Symmetry (e.g., Earthworm)

On the Basis of Germ Layers

  • Diploblastic: Animals with only two germ layers: Ectoderm (outermost germ layer) and Endoderm (innermost germ layer).
  • Triploblastic: Animals with three germ layers: Ectoderm, Mesoderm (middle germ layer), Endoderm.
  • E.g. Porifera, Coelenterate and Ctenophora are Diploblastic and rest all are Tribloblastic.

On the Basis of Coelom

  • → Coelom: It is the body cavity present between the body wall, and the gut wall. Coelom has a mesodermal lining.
  • Acoelomate: No coelom. E.g. Porifera, Coelenterate, Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes.
  • Pseudocoelomate: False coelom (body cavity not fully lined with mesoderm). E.g. Nematoda/Aschelminthes.
  • Eucoelomate: True coelom. E.g. Annelida, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Chordata.

Coelom: Acoelomate (Porifera/Coelenterata), Pseudocoelomate (Aschelminthes/Nematoda), Eucoelomate (Annelida to Chordata)

On the Basis of Circulatory System

  • Open Circulatory System: It is a system where there is no vessel to contain the blood and it flows freely through the cavities of the body. E.g. Arthropoda, Mollusca.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

Body segmentation refers to the division of an animal's body into repeating, similar units called segments. E.g. Seen in: Annelida, Arthropoda, Chordata.

  • Closed Circulatory System: It is a system where the blood is always contained within vessels in the heart while circulating. E.g. Annelida, Chordata.

Notochord

  • The notochord is a rod-like structure made of a cartilaginous substance that develops in all chordates at early embryonic stages as a rudimentary backbone.
  • It is derived from mesoderm.
  • It is present in the dorsal side (upper side or back side of an animal). E.g. Chordata.

Now let's learn about each phylum in details!

All Phylums in Order: Porifera, Coelenterate, Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda/Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Chordata

  1. 1. Phylum Porifera
  • Habitat: Mostly aquatic, marine, and a few freshwater species (E.g. Spongilla).
  • Body symmetry: Asymmetrical.
  • Body structure: Body is perforated with many tiny holes or pores (Ostium: Water canal system). Pores lead to a large central cavity called the Spongocoel. They have specialized "collar cells".
  • Level of organization: Cellular level organization (no true tissues or organs).
  • Germ layer: Diploblastic (endoderm and ectoderm).
  • Movement: Non-motile.
  • Endoskeleton is present.
  • They are hermaphrodites (posses both male and female reproductive system).

Other E.g. Euplectella (glass sponge), Scyon, Euspongia (bathing sponge).

  1. 2. Phylum Coelenterata/Cnidaria
  • Habitat: Aquatic, mostly marine, a few freshwater species (E.g. Hydra).
  • Symmetry: Radial symmetry.
  • Level of organization: Tissue level organization.
  • Germ layers: Diploblastic.
  • Body structure: Sac-like body with a central gastrovascular cavity (E.g. Coral, Hydra) having only one opening (hypostome) that serves as both mouth and anus. Tentacles surround the mouth, used for capturing food.
  • Special cells: Stinging cells called Cnidoblast contain a stinging capsule known as Nematocyst.
  • Hard skeleton is developed outside the body called Exoskeleton (made of calcium carbonate). E.g. Jellyfish, Aurelia.
  1. 3. Phylum Ctenophora
  • Habitat: Exclusively marine.
  • They exhibit bioluminescence.
  • Body symmetry: Radial symmetry.
  • They are also known as Sea Walnuts and Comb Jellies.
  • Reproduction: Sexual reproduction. They are hermaphrodites.

E.g. Pleurobrachia and Ctenoplana.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

  1. 4. Phylum Platyhelminthes
  • Body shape: Body is dorsoventrally flattened like a ribbon (flat from top to bottom). Suckers and hooks are present in few.
  • Habitat and nature: They are either free living or parasitic and terrestrial.
  • E.g. Planaria (free-living), Liverfluke (parasitic), Tapeworm.
  • Symmetry: Bilateral symmetry.
  • Germ layers: Triploblastic.
  • Level of organization: Organ level of organization (more advanced than Porifera and Coelenterata).
  • Coelom: Acoelomate.
  • Digestive system: Incomplete digestive system (common opening for both mouth and anus). Anus is absent.
  • Excretory system: Excretion and osmoregulation through specialized cells called flame cells.
  • They are hermaphrodites.
  1. 5. Phylum Aschelminthes/Nematodes
  • Body shape: Cylindrical, elongated, unsegmented body, tapered at both ends (spindle-shaped).
  • Symmetry: Bilateral symmetry.
  • Germ layers: Triploblastic.
  • Level of organization: Organ level of organization.
  • Coelom: Pseudocoelomate.
  • Habitat: Most forms are parasitic, but some are free living in soil or water.
  • Digestive system: Alimentary canal is complete (has both mouth and anus). Animals show sexual dimorphism (males and females look different). Mostly unisexual (male and female are separate).
  • Excretory system: Renette cells are present.

E.g. Ascaris (roundworm), Wuchereria (filarial worm), Ancyclostoma (hookworm).

  1. 6. Phylum Annelida
  • Body: Dorsoventrally flattened, cylindrical, segmentation is present on body.
  • Symmetry: Bilateral.
  • Germ layers: Triploblastic.
  • Coelom: Eucoelomate.
  • Level of organization: Organ system level.
  • Digestive System: Alimentary canal is tube like structure extended from mouth to anus.
  • Circulatory system: Closed (blood flows in vessels).
  • Locomotion: Through locomotory organs like parapodia (Nereis) that are lateral appendages.
  • Reproduction: Sexual, some are hermaphrodites, some show asexual reproduction.
  • Excretory system: Nephridia is present for osmoregulation and excretion.

E.g. Earthworms, Leech, Nereis, Hirudinaria, etc.

  1. 7. Phylum Arthropoda
  • Largest phylum in Animal Kingdom → Insecta is the largest class.
  • Body: Segmented into head, thorax, and abdomen. They have joint appendages (jointed legs).
  • Exoskeleton: Made of chitin.
  • Symmetry: Bilateral.
  • Coelom: True, filled with blood.
  • Habitat: Terrestrial, aquatic, fresh or marine animals.
  • Germ layer: Triploblastic.
  • Circulatory System: Open circulatory system.
  • Respiration through: Gills, trachea, or book lungs.
  • Excretion through: Malpighian tubules.
  • Reproduction: Mostly unisexual, sexual dimorphism is common.
  • Digestive system: Alimentary canal is complete.

E.g. Spider, scorpio, crab, silver fish, cray fish, etc.

  1. 8. Phylum Mollusca
  • It is the second largest phylum of Animal Kingdom.
  • Body: Soft, little segmentation. The body is divided into head, foot, and in mantle (a fold of thin skin).
  • Covering: Most have a calcareous shell (snails).
  • Symmetry: Bilateral.

PLANT AND ANIMAL KINGDOM

  • Coelom: Eucoelomate.
  • Circulatory System: Mostly open; closed in octopus and squid.
  • Respiration: Gills or lungs.
  • Digestive system: Alimentary canal is complete.
  • Excretory system: Kidney-like organs called nephridia is present for excretion.
  • Reproduction: Unisexual, external or internal fertilization.
  • They have blue color blood due to Haemocyanin.

E.g. Octopus, snails (pila), oysters, squid, etc.

  1. 9. Phylum Echinodermata
  • Body: Star-shaped, spherical, elongated. They are spiny-skinned organisms with no segmentation on body.
  • Symmetry: Radial.
  • Coelom: Eucoelomate.
  • Germ layer: Triploblastic.
  • System of organization: Organ system. E.g. Sea urchins, starfish, Holothuria, sea cucumber.
  1. 10. Phylum Chordata
  • They have a notochord (rod-like supportive structure).
  • They have pharyngeal gill slits in pharynx.
  • Heart is ventral.
  • Circulatory system: Closed circulatory system.
  • Coelom: Eucoelomate.
  • Symmetry: Bilateral.
  • Germ layer: Triploblastic.
  • Level of organization: Organ level of organization.
  • Phylum Chordata is divided into two major groups: Protochordata and Vertebrata.

Protochordata have notochord, but never form a verbal column.

Remember: Hemichordata is not a sub-phylum under Chordata. It consists of small group of worm like animals.

Characteristics of Protochordata

  • They do not have proper notochord (present only in larval stage or not well developed).
  • No vertebral column, post anal tail present.
  • Bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate.
  • Nerve cord is present.
  • Germ layer: Triploblastic.
  • Pharyngeal gill slits present.

Classes of Vertebrates

  1. 1. Cyclostomata
  • They are jawless vertebrates.
  • They have elongated eel-like body, circular mouth, and slimy skin.
  • E.g. Petromyzon/Myxine, hog fishes, lamprey.
  1. 2. Pisces
  • They are fishes. E.g Dog fish, shark, tuna, sea horse, etc.
  • Pieces have two-chambered heart.
  1. 3. Amphibians
  • They use mucous glands or gills for respiration.
  • They have three-chambered heart.
  • They are cold blooded animals.
  • They breathe through lungs or gills (in water) and skin (in land).
  • E.g. Frogs, toads, salamander.
  1. 4. Reptiles
  • They have three-chambered heart [exception: Crocodile (has four-chambered heart)].
  • They are cold blooded animals.
  • They breathe through their lungs.
  • E.g. Snake, turtle, lizard, crocodile, chameleon.
  1. 5. Aves (Birds)
  • They have four-chambered heart.
  • They are warm blooded.
  • They lay eggs (oviparous).
  1. 6. Mammals
  • They have four-chambered heart.
  • They are warm blooded.
  • They have mammary glands (viviparous). Exception: Platypus and echidnas (lay eggs).
  • E.g. Dolphin, whale, humans, etc.
